French Interior Ministry investigates racist messages at national police academy in Cannes-Ecluse, with two officer cadets suspended and facing disciplinary proceedings after Le Parisien reported the exchange of racist caricatures and Nazi imagery among trainees.

## What happened

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez confirmed on Monday that an administrative investigation had been launched at the National Police Academy in Cannes-Ecluse following reports of racist messages circulated among officer cadets. According to Nunez, approximately 30 students were interviewed as part of the inquiry, which led to the identification of two officer cadets as primarily implicated in the incidents.

The investigation was initiated after Le Parisien reported that racist messages, caricatures, and photographs—including an image depicting a Nazi salute—had been exchanged in private conversations among trainees at the academy. Nunez stated that "the first has been suspended and his situation will be examined by the academic board. The second is subject to disciplinary proceedings."

The Interior Ministry escalated the matter to judicial authorities under Article 40 of France's Code of Criminal Procedure. The prosecutor's office in Fontainebleau opened a preliminary investigation, and the National Police Inspectorate (IGPN)—France's police oversight body—was notified of the case.

## Reaction

Interior Minister Nunez issued a statement condemning the conduct in the "strongest possible terms." "I strongly condemn, in the strongest possible terms, the unacceptable remarks and conduct, which have no place, even less so in an institution responsible for training future officers of the national police," he said via X (formerly Twitter). The academy's management launched the administrative investigation immediately upon learning of the incidents, according to Nunez's account.

## Why it matters

The incident highlights ongoing concerns about racism and extremist ideology within French law enforcement institutions. The National Police Academy serves as the primary training ground for France's future police officers, making standards of conduct and vetting procedures particularly significant for public trust in policing. The dual administrative and judicial response signals official recognition of the seriousness of the allegations and reflects broader French efforts to address racist conduct within state institutions.

## Background

The National Police Academy (École Nationale de Police) in Cannes-Ecluse, located southeast of Paris, trains officer cadets for France's national police force. The IGPN, formally known as the Inspection Générale de la Police Nationale, functions as France's internal police accountability mechanism, investigating allegations of police misconduct. Article 40 of France's Code of Criminal Procedure allows officials to report potential criminal offenses to judicial authorities, triggering formal investigation procedures. France's secular legal framework (laïcité) emphasizes equal treatment regardless of religion or ethnic background, making discrimination cases subject to both administrative and criminal sanction.

---

**What specific racist content was reported to have circulated among the cadets?**

According to Le Parisien's reporting cited by Interior Minister Nunez, the exchanged materials included racist messages, caricatures, photographs, and an image depicting a Nazi salute. The academy's management did not publicly detail the full scope of the racist material when confirming the investigation.

**What are the potential consequences for the two identified officer cadets?**

The first cadet has been suspended, with his status to be examined by the academic board. The second cadet is currently subject to disciplinary proceedings. Both may face additional consequences depending on outcomes of the ongoing judicial investigation and IGPN review.

**Which authorities are investigating the incidents?**

The academy's internal administration conducted the initial inquiry. The prosecutor's office in Fontainebleau opened a preliminary investigation, and the National Police Inspectorate (IGPN) was notified and is involved in the ongoing investigation.

**When was the incident brought to public attention?**

French newspaper Le Parisien first reported the racist messages and imagery exchanged among officer cadets. Interior Minister Nunez's public statement confirming the investigation was made on Monday, 24 November 2026.

Sources: Anadolu Agency, French Interior Ministry (statement via Laurent Nunez)

# Nanterre Prefecture Orders Ibn Badis Institute to Stop Teaching Minors in New Administrative Clash

The Hauts-de-Seine prefecture has banned the Ibn Badis Institute in Nanterre from hosting minors for extracurricular activities, effective Sunday, 22 November, following a departmental inspection. The institute has announced it will contest the order in administrative court while complying with the directive, claiming the prefecture is subjecting it to "administrative harassment."

## What happened

A prefectural order issued by the Hauts-de-Seine prefecture on 22 November prohibits the Ibn Badis Institute from welcoming minors for extracurricular activities, immediately halting Arabic language courses and religious instruction for children at the facility. The ban followed a control inspection conducted that same week by the Departmental Service for Youth, Civic Engagement and Sports (SDJES).

The Ibn Badis Institute responded swiftly to the order. In a statement, the institute declared: "We will apply this order, as we are committed to respecting the law, but we will contest it with the utmost firmness." The institute announced it has filed an urgent referral with the administrative tribunal to challenge the prefecture's decision.

## Dispute over classification

The core disagreement centres on how the prefecture classifies the institute's activities. According to the Ibn Badis Institute, the prefecture is treating the Arabic language and religious education courses as collective youth reception activities (ACM—accueils collectifs de mineurs) subject to formal declaration and regulatory oversight. The institute contests this characterization, arguing instead that "the activities in question are primarily educational and religious transmission activities, designed to allow children to learn their religion, discover their values and develop their [knowledge of their faith]."

## Reaction

The Nanterre municipal authorities have questioned the prefecture's decision, with the city suggesting the administrative action represents "administrative harassment" directed at the Ibn Badis Institute. The city has not yet announced whether it will publicly support the institute's legal challenge.

## Why it matters

This dispute reflects ongoing tensions in France over how municipal and prefectural authorities regulate religious education facilities, particularly those serving Muslim communities. The case raises questions about the distinction between religious instruction and youth welfare regulations, and whether such classifications disproportionately affect Muslim-led institutions. The outcome could influence how similar facilities nationwide are regulated under French administrative law.

## Background

The Ibn Badis Institute is a cultural and educational association in Nanterre, a working-class suburb northwest of Paris in the Hauts-de-Seine department. France's prefectural system gives prefects—appointed state representatives—significant authority over local administrative matters, including licensing and regulation of youth activities. Extracurricular youth activities in France typically fall under ACM regulations, which mandate formal declaration, trained staff, and compliance with safety and welfare standards. Religious organisations offering education to minors sometimes dispute whether their activities qualify as ACM-regulated services or fall instead under religious instruction exemptions, creating recurring administrative conflicts. The prefecture's authority to issue such orders and the institut's right to challenge them through the administrative court (tribunal administratif) are established aspects of French administrative procedure.

Sources: Saphirnews

---

**Who issued the ban and when did it take effect?**

The Hauts-de-Seine prefecture issued the prefectural order on 22 November 2026, and it took effect immediately that same day, prohibiting the Ibn Badis Institute from hosting minors for extracurricular activities.

**What specific activities are affected?**

Arabic language courses and religious education classes for children offered by the Ibn Badis Institute as extracurricular activities have been halted under the order.

**What is the Ibn Badis Institute's legal argument?**

The institute argues that its activities constitute religious education and transmission of faith values, not collective youth reception activities (ACM), and therefore should not be subject to ACM regulations and formal declaration requirements that the prefecture is enforcing.

**How has the municipal government responded?**

The Nanterre municipal authorities have questioned the prefectural decision as potentially constituting "administrative harassment" directed at the Ibn Badis Institute, though the city has not formally committed to supporting the institute's legal challenge.

Green Party deputy Sabrina Sebaihi has condemned what she describes as a pattern of closures affecting Muslim organisations in France, following a prefectural order against the Institut Ibn Badis in Nanterre that prohibits the school from hosting minors in extracurricular activities. The measure, issued after an inspection by the departmental youth and sports service, has been contested in administrative court by the institute's lawyer, Maître Guez Guez.

## What happened

The Institut Ibn Badis, a Muslim school in Nanterre in the Hauts-de-Seine département, received a prefectural order on 21 November that banned it from welcoming minors during extracurricular activities, according to a statement published by the institute on that date. The decision followed an inspection by the Service départemental à la jeunesse, à l'engagement et aux sports (SDJES), the departmental service responsible for youth, civic engagement, and sports.

The core dispute concerns how the institute's activities should be classified. The prefectural authorities argue that the activities fall under regulations governing collective youth facilities (accueils collectifs de mineurs, or ACM), which are subject to specific regulatory requirements. The Institut Ibn Badis contests this characterisation, maintaining through its legal representation that its activities primarily constitute religious education and transmission rather than regulated youth facilities.

The institute announced its intention to challenge the order through emergency proceedings in the administrative tribunal, with its lawyer filing the dispute.

## Reaction

On 23 November, deputy Sabrina Sebaihi, who represents Nanterre, issued a statement calling for dialogue and alerting public attention to what she characterises as a broader pattern of closures affecting Muslim structures in France. According to TSA Algerie, Sebaihi has described an escalating climate of Islamophobic acts and racist measures. The statement references concerns previously raised by the Grande Mosquée de Paris and its rector, Chems-Eddine Hafiz, regarding what they have identified as pervasive Islamophobia affecting Muslim communities in the country.

## Why it matters

The case reflects ongoing tensions in France over the treatment of Muslim organisations and raises questions about the application of youth facility regulations to religious educational institutions. For Muslim communities in France, the incident illustrates concerns about disproportionate regulatory scrutiny. The dispute also touches on broader debates in France around laïcité—the principle of state secularism—and how regulations governing youth services interact with religious educational activities.

## Background

The Institut Ibn Badis is an Islamic school operating in Nanterre, a commune in the western suburbs of Paris. France has experienced heightened political debate over Islam, secularism, and Muslim civic participation in recent years, with disputes frequently centring on how regulations apply to Muslim-led institutions. The SDJES operates at the departmental level to oversee youth facilities and services. Administrative tribunals in France handle disputes between citizens and public authorities, including prefectural orders.

Sabrina Sebaihi, an ecologist deputy representing Nanterre, sits in the French National Assembly. Her intervention reflects growing parliamentary scrutiny of regulatory actions affecting Muslim organisations.

The institute announced receipt of the order on 21 November, according to its published statement.

The institute's lawyer, Maître Guez Guez, filed emergency proceedings (référé) with the administrative tribunal to contest the order.

**What is the legal disagreement at the heart of this case?**

The prefectural authorities classify the activities as regulated youth collective facilities (ACM), subject to specific requirements. The institute argues its activities constitute religious education and transmission, which fall outside that regulatory framework.
